doc.title: Bill Easley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 1, 2021

title: Teaching as language and lesson one from Joe Allard
summary: He would like to teach, stresses the space between the notes, and gives Allard's chromatic interval exercise as lesson one.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Okay. You said — that’s a great story. You said something a couple of minutes ago that I want to follow up on. When he was asking you about the bridge to “I Got Rhythm” and you said basically that I know what to do but I don’t necessarily know what it is I’m doing. And in this day of intense jazz education where you can study for years and get a Ph.D., I’m wondering how that mindset jives with what we’re teaching now?

Well see I — at this late stage in my life I’d like to teach. But see like people in academia avoid me like the plague. You know? They have no interest in me, even though I’ve done this for sixty-some years. And I’ve pretty much accepted that by now. But I’ve had a couple of students near home, they come to my house, and I’m trying to teach as a language more so than a technical — even though see what Sonny Stitt told me about don’t worry about it, I didn’t — that does not mean that no, you shouldn’t learn. The more information that you have the better off you are. But there’s different kinds of ways to approach any subject man, there’s various different parts of the brain that deal with it this way or this way. You can do the same thing in different ways. You have an intellectual approach to it or you have a certain thing playing by ear — what does that mean and so on and so on. So, because in fact the notes are not the problem it’s the space between ‘em [gap] and everything else. It’s not how your birth date and your death date, it’s about all that space in between or how do you get from here to Chicago. You know it’s [waves arm]. So that’s what music is or any language. It’s about the space between. And so that’s what sometimes people don’t necessarily pay attention to but it’s the most important thing. It’s about that space between. That’s again, I’m not looking for a teaching position or anything like that but I do enjoy teaching in the same way that I’ve © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

always taught. I’m not saying I never taught because over the years somebody wanted to, “Man I’d like to study with you, I’d like to study.” So well the first problem I have, I don’t know what to charge you because I’ve never been a teacher so I don’t know what to charge. So lesson one is free. You come to my house and I’ll give you what I think is lesson one. I won’t charge. And lesson one is a lesson that I got from Joe Allard way back in 1964, you understand? Joe Allard who had you take your instrument, clarinet or saxophone or it applies on any instrument. And he’d take you through a chromatic sequence of intervals. Now you’d start with a major second up, minor second down, major [scats] you know, a chromatic sequence of intervals. You do seconds, minor seconds up and down. Then expand it. Minor third up, minor third — you know, major second down. A fifth up, you know, diminished fifth down. You know, one note to the next, any music ideas start with two notes [scats]. So the whole thing is mastering one note to the next. And so I would tell the student, now listen, this is something you’ll never master but it’s something you have to keep working on for the rest of your life. Now we can take that same concept and we can expand upon it and we could write a book as thick as two telephone books, we take and we build major thirds on that movement. Or any four note motif that you come up with, and take it through that cycle in other words and put it in your head and run it through — you know put it on your horn. So that’s — it’s very basic information and I always do that as lesson one. Nobody ever came back for lesson two, so I never made a dime, you understand? They’d never come back. And I’d see them thirty years later, “Oh man, I’m still working on it.” I say well I told you you’ll still work on it, but there’s more information actually. But very few people want to come. I’ve got a student now, and he’s in another, he’s a scientist. He prides himself as taking the most consecutive lessons from me, which is four. You understand? He’s trying to break anybody’s record, man.
